title: Multimedia Presentations
keyIdea: Multimedia components (pictures, charts, maps, sound and video) and visual displays such as slides belong in a presentation when they help develop a main idea or theme. Choose the medium that fits the information: a chart for numbers that change or compare, a map or plan for where things are, a photo for what something looks like, a sound or video clip for what something sounds like or how it moves, and nothing at all for a simple fact you can say. A slide shows a title and key words, not your script. Cut anything that distracts, and show each visual at the moment you reach its point.
familyTip: Before a school talk, ask your child to say each main point in one sentence, then ask: what would help someone see this? For each picture or chart they choose, ask which point it shows. If it shows none, leave it out. Practise once with the slides and check each one appears when they reach its point.

visual.caption: Does each extra help the main idea or distract from it? Drag each card, or tap it and then a box.

items: A chart of the pond's width each year
Music playing under the whole talk
A map showing where the reeds will go
Words that spin onto the slide
A cute cat on a slide about ponds
Captions on a video with speech

lab.caption: Flagship lab: give each point its visual, cut a slide to key words, remove distractions, pick the media and time each slide.

kid: A talk can use more than your voice. You can add pictures, charts, maps, sounds or short videos, often on slides. These are called multimedia. Each one should help your listeners understand a main point.

Pick the kind that fits. Numbers that change over time are clearer on a chart. A place is clearer on a map. A sound is best as a short clip. How something looks is best as a photo. A simple fact, like the day a club meets, needs nothing extra.
A slide is not your script. If every word is on the slide, people read instead of listening. Put a title and a few key words or numbers. Then say the rest yourself.

Some extras pull attention away from your idea. Spinning words, music under your voice and pictures that are not about the point all distract. Ask of each one: which point does this help? If the answer is none, cut it. Timing matters too. Show each visual when you reach its point. If a map is up while you talk about frogs, people look at the map and stop listening.
adult: Ages 10 to 11. This is the Common Core speaking and listening standard SL.5.5: include multimedia components (e.g. graphics, sound) and visual displays in presentations when appropriate to enhance the development of main ideas or themes (SL.4.5 is the grade 4 version with audio recordings). It supports the KS2 spoken language statements in the National Curriculum in England on giving well-structured presentations and gaining, maintaining and monitoring the interest of listeners.

The lab uses a made-up Year 6 talk, Save our school pond. Learners drag the visual that shows each of three points (and find that a cute cat shows none), cut a slide that copies the script down to the title and key numbers, remove three distractions while keeping the chart, labels and title, choose the media for five kinds of information, and show five slides in step with the script.

Common mistakes. Children add pictures because they look nice rather than because they show a point, copy the whole script onto slides and read it out, pile on animations and background music, use a chart or video where a sentence would do, and leave a slide up after they have moved on. Ask them to name the point each visual helps; if they cannot, it goes.

practice.prompt: Sam's point is: "The pond was 4 m wide in 2023 and is 2 m wide now." Which visual helps most?
choices: A bar chart of the width each year
A cute photo of a frog
The whole sentence typed on the slide
practice.hint: The point is about a number that changed. Which visual shows numbers changing?
practice.explain: A bar chart shows the width shrinking from 4 m to 2 m at a glance. The frog is not about the width, and a typed sentence just repeats what Sam says.

practice.prompt: A slide has {k} key words and {e} extra words that Sam will say out loud anyway. How many words should be cut from the slide?
practice.hint: Keep the key words. Cut the words Sam is going to say out loud anyway.
practice.explain: Cut the {e} extra words and keep the {k} key words. Sam says the rest, so listeners look and listen at once.

practice.prompt: Which piece of information is best shown on a map?
choices: Where the new reeds will be planted
How loud the frogs are at night
How many bottles were collected each month
practice.hint: A map shows where things are.
practice.explain: Where the reeds go is a place, so a map or plan shows it best. A sound needs a clip, and amounts each month suit a chart.

practice.prompt: A talk has {p} main points. Each point gets one visual, and the talk also has a title slide and a thank-you slide. How many slides is that?
practice.hint: Count one slide for each point, then add the title slide and the thank-you slide.
practice.explain: {p} point slides + 1 title slide + 1 thank-you slide = {=p+2} slides.

practice.prompt: When should Sam show the map of where the reeds will go?
choices: While he talks about the reeds
From the very start of the talk
After he has finished the talk
practice.hint: A visual helps most when people see it at the same time as they hear the point.
practice.explain: Show the map while Sam talks about the reeds. Too early, people study it instead of listening; too late, the point is over.

pool.prompt: Which is the best slide for a talk?
choices: A title, a few key words and one clear picture
Every word you will say, in small writing
Lots of pictures and spinning words
pool.hint: The slide should support your voice, not replace it or compete with it.
pool.explain: A title, key words and one clear picture support the talk. A full script makes people read instead of listen, and spinning words distract.

pool.prompt: Should you play music behind your whole talk?
choices: No, it makes your voice harder to follow
Yes, it keeps people awake
Yes, as long as it is loud
pool.hint: Think about what listeners need to hear clearly.
pool.explain: Music under your voice competes with your words, so it distracts from the main idea.

pool.prompt: Your point is "Frogs croak loudly at night." Which media fits best?
choices: A short sound clip
A bar chart
A map of the pond
pool.hint: The point is about a sound.
pool.explain: A sound clip lets listeners hear the croaking. A chart shows amounts and a map shows places.

pool.prompt: A picture of a cute puppy would make your pond slide prettier. Should you add it?
choices: No, it does not show a point of the talk
Yes, people like puppies
Yes, if it is small
pool.hint: Ask which main point the picture helps.
pool.explain: The puppy shows none of the points about the pond, so it pulls attention away from the idea.

pool.prompt: A slide has {a} pictures that show the point and {b} pictures that are just decoration. How many should you remove?
pool.hint: Keep the pictures that show the point. Remove the ones that are only decoration.
pool.explain: Remove the {b} decorations and keep the {a} pictures that show the point.

pool.prompt: Your video clip has people talking. How can you help listeners who cannot hear it well?
choices: Turn on captions
Play it louder all the time
Show it with the sound off
pool.hint: How could people follow the words without hearing them?
pool.explain: Captions show the spoken words on screen, so everyone can follow. Louder sound can drown out the room and does not help everyone.

pool.prompt: Your point is "The pond club meets on Tuesdays." What should you add?
choices: Nothing, just say it
A bar chart of the days
A video of a calendar
pool.hint: Does a simple fact need a picture to be understood?
pool.explain: A simple fact is clear when you say it. Adding a chart or video would only distract.

pool.prompt: Your slide has a long paragraph on it. What should you do?
choices: Cut it to key words and say the rest
Read the paragraph out loud
Make the writing smaller
pool.hint: Who should do the talking: you or the slide?
pool.explain: Cut it to key words and say the rest. Reading a paragraph aloud makes listeners read along, and small writing cannot be read from the back.

pool.prompt: Sam's talk has {p} main points. Two of them are simple facts he can just say. How many points need a visual?
pool.hint: Simple facts need no media. Take them away from the number of points.
pool.explain: {p} points − 2 simple facts = {=p-2} points that need a visual, one for each.
